title: Statistical Arbitrage
answer: Statistical arbitrage is a quantitative trading approach that looks for relative value between related securities, often using statistical models to identify temporary mispricings. It typically involves a large number of positions, short holding periods, and a market-neutral stance, though neutrality is a target rather than a guarantee. In the context of AI-related markets, the universe can include the 117 listed AI-related instruments with daily prices that this site tracks, alongside broader equities, ETFs, and derivatives. The strategy sits within quantitative trading and relies on data, computation, and execution rather than on company fundamentals alone.

sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: The work runs on a data and execution stack that includes historical and real-time market data, a research environment for backtesting, and a low-latency connection to brokers or exchanges. Storage and compute are often cloud-based, with time-series databases and distributed processing for large datasets. Risk systems monitor exposures, leverage, and drawdown in real time, and they can automatically reduce positions when limits are breached. For AI-related instruments, daily prices and corporate actions feed the research pipeline, while intraday data and order book feeds are common for live trading.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: The process starts with data cleaning and feature construction, then moves to signal generation using techniques such as cointegration, principal component analysis, or machine learning models. Portfolios are built to be dollar neutral or beta neutral, with position sizing based on volatility and correlation estimates. Execution algorithms slice orders to reduce market impact, and the strategy is monitored for decay in predictive power. Backtests must account for transaction costs, borrow costs, and survivorship bias, because these can turn an apparently profitable signal into a losing one.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance cover market data licensing, model documentation, and the audit trail for every trade. Firms need to know where data comes from, whether it was legally obtained, and how it is permitted to be used, especially for alternative data. Model risk management includes validation, ongoing monitoring, and a clear process for retiring a model that stops working. Regulatory obligations touch on market conduct, short selling rules, and reporting, and they vary by jurisdiction and instrument type.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The field is moving toward more machine learning, alternative data, and automated feature discovery, which raises the bar for infrastructure and governance. Competition has compressed returns in simple pairs trading, so firms look to faster execution, more instruments, and better risk models. Capacity constraints mean that successful strategies tend to be scaled carefully, and crowded trades can unwind quickly. Regulatory attention to algorithmic trading and data use is likely to keep growing, shaping what can be built and how it is documented.
